prompt.context: Our client is one of the top three beverage manufacturers in the US. They are a vertically integrated beverage manufacturer that makes the drinks, has five bottling plants, and owns their own distribution channels.
prompt.question: The company is thinking of launching a new non-sparkling flavored water product. They have asked us to determine whether or not they should launch the new product, how to do it, and what the marketing strategy should be.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of the entire water market?
What is the breakdown of the water market between sparkling and non-sparkling?
clarifying_info.a: 90% sparkling, 10% non-sparkling (flavored water). Within the non-sparkling segment, O2 Flavor holds 18%, Easy Drink holds 12%, and Others hold 70%.

clarifying_info.q: How will the drinks be packaged?
clarifying_info.a: Everyone packages their water in 16oz bottles, and our client will do the same.

clarifying_info.q: How will the drink be priced?
What are the costs per bottle?
What is the total launch cost?

exhibits.title: Water Market Breakdown: Sparkling vs Non-Sparkling, and Flavored Water Competitors
exhibits.shows: Two pie charts: the first shows the split of the overall water market between sparkling and non-sparkling; the second shows the market share breakdown within the non-sparkling flavored water segment among named competitors and others

exhibits.title: Competitor Positioning: How Consumers Perceive Flavored Water Products
exhibits.shows: A horizontal bar chart showing the percentage of survey respondents who associate each of the main flavored water brands (O2 Flavor, Easy Drink, Other) with three positioning categories: low-calorie healthy drink, sports drink, and leisure beverage

framework: Define the market: size the overall water market and the relevant non-sparkling flavored water sub-segment
Assess the competitive landscape: identify existing players, their market shares, and positioning
Size the opportunity: calculate market size in units and revenue potential for the client
Evaluate economics: determine margins, break-even volume, and payback period
Develop go-to-market strategy: recommend product positioning, target segment, and marketing approach
Identify risks: consider market trends, cannibalization, and execution challenges
Make a recommendation: synthesize findings into a clear go/no-go with conditions

questions.prompt: What is the size of the flavored non-sparkling water market in bottles per year?
questions.guidance: Candidate should start from the total water market (8 million gallons), apply the 10% non-sparkling share, then convert gallons to 16oz bottles using the conversion factor (4 bottles per gallon).

math.setup: Total water market = 8M gallons/year; non-sparkling share = 10%; bottle size = 16oz; 1 gallon = 128oz so 128/16 = 8 bottles per gallon — wait, casebook uses 64oz per gallon (likely a simplified assumption): 64oz/16oz = 4 bottles per gallon
steps: Non-sparkling flavored water market = 10% x 8,000,000 gallons = 800,000 gallons/year
Convert to bottles: 800,000 gallons x 4 bottles/gallon = 3,200,000 bottles/year
math.answer: 3.2 million bottles sold per year in the flavored non-sparkling water market

questions.prompt: Given a launch cost of $400,000 and a margin of $0.10 per bottle, how many bottles must the client sell to break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the per-bottle contribution margin (price minus cost) and divide the fixed launch investment by that margin. The key insight is that the break-even volume exceeds the entire annual market.

math.setup: Price = $1.00/bottle; Cost = $0.90/bottle; Contribution margin = $0.10/bottle; Fixed launch cost = $400,000
math.answer: 4 million bottles must be sold to break even — which is larger than the entire annual market of 3.2 million bottles

questions.prompt: Assuming the client captures a 15% market share, how many years will it take to break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use the market share data from the competitor exhibit to justify a reasonable market share assumption. Since the two main competitors hold 18% and 12%, a new entrant backed by a major company might capture roughly 15%. The key insight is that 8 years is a very long payback period for the beverage industry.

math.setup: Annual market = 3.2 million bottles; assumed market share = 15%; break-even volume = 4 million bottles
steps: Annual bottles sold by client = 15% x 3,200,000 = 480,000 bottles ≈ 0.5 million bottles/year
math.answer: Approximately 8 years to break even — an extremely long payback period for the beverage industry

brainstorming.prompt: What problems or risks should the client consider with this new venture?

categories.name: Market / Industry Risks
ideas: Flavored water may be a passing fad — trends in the beverage market change rapidly
Overall non-sparkling market is small (only 10% of the water market) and highly fragmented
New entrants could also emerge, intensifying competition

categories.name: Internal / Cannibalization Risks
ideas: Cannibalization of the client's existing beverage products
Resource allocation: the client's five bottling plants and distribution channels may need to be redirected from existing products
Brand dilution if the new product does not fit the client's existing identity

categories.name: Execution Risks
ideas: 8-year break-even suggests high execution risk if market conditions change
Marketing and positioning challenges in a crowded 'other' category
Pricing power may be limited at $1/bottle given thin margins

recommendation: The launch is questionable given the 8-year break-even — a very long horizon for the fast-moving beverage industry

However, if interest in flavored non-sparkling water remains strong and the client can leverage its brand, vertical integration, and distribution network to rapidly capture 15%+ market share, the product has long-term profit potential
risks: Flavored water trend fades before break-even is reached
Cannibalization of existing products erodes net benefit
Competitive response from O2 Flavor and Easy Drink compresses margins or market share
next_steps: Conduct consumer research to validate demand durability and preferred positioning (sports drink vs. leisure beverage)
Model scenarios with higher market share capture (e.g., 20-25%) to assess whether break-even can be shortened to 4-5 years
Assess cannibalization impact on existing product portfolio before committing to launch
